script: This chapter is about your first steps in Scratch, a place where you build stories with blocks that snap together like LEGO bricks. In these lessons you meet the cat, learn to move and talk, and learn to change costumes. Each lesson adds a new block or idea to your script, so you build your story step by step.

The Stage is the picture area where your story happens. The cat is a sprite, which is a character in your story. The Stage, the sprite, the Blocks palette, and the Code area are the parts you use in Scratch. You see the cat on the Stage, and you find blocks in the Blocks palette to drag into the Code area.

Blocks live in the Blocks palette, and you drag them into the Code area to build a script. A script is a stack of blocks in the Code area. You build a script by snapping blocks together, one under another. The blocks snap together like LEGO bricks, so they stay in order.

The green flag starts a script, and the red stop sign stops it. For example, drag when green flag clicked into the Code area. Snap move ten steps under it, so the script has two blocks. When you click the green flag, the cat moves ten steps, and the red stop sign stops the script.

In the next lesson, you learn to move and talk. The block move ten steps moves the sprite ten steps. The block say Hello for two seconds shows a speech bubble with the words Hello. The cat says Hello for two seconds, and then the speech bubble goes away.

Blocks run from top to bottom in a script. For example, first move ten steps, then say Hello for two seconds, then move ten more steps. The cat moves, then talks, then moves again, so the total is twenty steps. Steps are distance, and seconds are time, so ten steps is a distance and two seconds is a time.

A costume is a picture of a sprite. One sprite can have many costumes, and the cat has two costumes. The block next costume goes to the next picture. The block switch costume to picks an exact picture, so you can choose which costume to show.

The cat has two costumes, so next costume changes the picture from one to the other. The block wait zero point five seconds makes a short pause. Small waits make the change easy to see, because the new picture stays for a moment. This helps when you want a visible animation, so the change is not too fast.

Remember three things. First, blocks snap into scripts, and the green flag starts a script while the red stop sign stops it. Second, move ten steps moves the sprite ten steps, say Hello for two seconds shows a speech bubble, and steps are distance while seconds are time. Third, a costume is a picture, next costume changes to the next picture, switch costume to picks an exact picture, and a small wait makes the change easy to see.

script: This chapter is about making a story in Scratch, and you learn three big ideas that help your story work. You learn how scenes and backdrops work, how loops repeat actions, and how to add a score. Each lesson gives you a small piece, and each piece helps your story run the way you plan.

First, scenes and backdrops. A backdrop is the background picture on the Stage, and a scene is one part of a story. A scene has a backdrop, sprites, and words or actions, so the backdrop is the picture behind everything and the sprites and words or actions are the parts that happen in that place. For example, the Park scene uses the Park backdrop, and the Beach scene uses the Beach backdrop.

Use switch backdrop to change the background. Use wait three seconds to hold the Park scene, which keeps the Park backdrop on the Stage for three seconds, then switch to Beach. The story has two scenes, so you change from the Park backdrop to the Beach backdrop, and you use switch backdrop to change the background, not switch costume.

Next, repeat with loops. A loop repeats the blocks inside it, and loops save space because you do not need to copy the same blocks many times. Repeat five runs the inside blocks five times, and it counts one, two, three, four, five, then stops. Only the blocks inside the loop repeat, so if a block is outside the loop, it does not repeat with the loop.

Here is a tiny example. The cat moves five steps four times, and that is twenty steps in all because five and five and five and five make twenty. The cat waits half a second four times, and that is two seconds in all. The loop does the inside blocks again and again, and then it stops after the set number of times.

Now add a score. A variable is a box that holds a number, and the number can change while the story runs. Click the green flag, then use set score to zero, so the score starts at zero. That means the score begins at zero each time you start the story, and starting at zero helps you count points from the beginning.

Click the cat, then use change score by one, and each click adds one point. The new score is the old score plus one, so use change, not set, to add points. Change keeps the old score and adds one, so each click makes the score one bigger and the score counts up as you click.

Here are the three things to remember. First, a scene has a backdrop, sprites, and words or actions, and you change the background with switch backdrop. Second, a loop repeats only the blocks inside it, and loops save space. Third, a score variable starts at zero, and change score by one adds a point, because the new score is the old score plus one.
